202701:23272.text: This comprehensive course in Biostatistics is designed to cultivate expertise in both theoretical concepts and practical applications. Throughout the year-long program, participants will develop the skills needed to employ statistical analyses for diverse data sets and research studies. These include descriptive statistics, bivariate comparisons, multivariable analyses encompassing linear and logistic regression, survival analysis, and specialized topics such as hierarchical modeling, Poisson regression, repeated measures and time series analyses, weighting and complex survey design, as well as difference-in-differences, propensity score and instrumental variables analyses. By the course's conclusion, participants will be adept at not only conducting bivariate and multivariable statistical analyses but also critiquing and interpreting statistical methods frequently used in the medical journal literature. During the spring term, students will apply statistical modeling techniques with exposure to an array of advanced topics including methods for analyzing categorical dependent variables, quasi-experimental designs, and panel/correlated data as well as risk model development and validation, psychometrics and exploratory factor analysis, and survey weighting schemes. Classes will meet for 2 hours once a week with labs covering most topics. See updated spring Assessments include regular lab applications, homework, and quizzes to assess progress and reinforce concepts. Permission of the instructor required.

202701:23273.text: This research methodologies course incorporates quantitative and qualitative approaches. Participants learn to design diverse clinical and health services research studies, covering study design, sampling, data collection, and analysis. Summer sessions focus on quantitative methods, fall for qualitative, and advanced topics in spring. The summer course is an intensive, program that provides a comprehensive core concepts and methods in clinical epidemiology. Topics include measurements of disease frequency and association, study design (including randomized and non-randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, and ecologic studies), screening principles, reliability and validity, bias, confounding, and effect modification. The qualitative content provides a comprehensive overview of the theoretical and practical concepts and methods for conducting qualitative research in public health, nursing, and medicine. The course aspires to introduce scholars to various epistemological, philosophical, and ethical considerations that are involved with qualitative research methods. Additionally, scholars gain practical knowledge of strategies and techniques that are needed to conduct qualitative research. Topics include qualitative designs, mixed methods, theories and frameworks, sampling, rigor, data coding and analysis, data saturation, ethical considerations, writing for publication, and writing for grants and other products. After completing this course scholars will be able to design a qualitative study and evaluate the qualitative literature in their field. Permission of the instructor required.

This is a course in development economics with a particular focus on understanding and measuring inclusive development and on assessing policies to promote inclusive development. This framing is applied to understanding post-apartheid South Africa’s development record and undertaking a quantitative assessment of policies that have been implemented in South Africa over this period. Classes include data labs introducing participants to the measurement of inequality, poverty, and inclusive development using relevant South African datasets. There is a lab test. Classes also include discussions of relevant literature on inclusive development and relevant South African literature. During spring break, all travel to South Africa with Professor Leibbrandt to undertake structured engagements with those involved in policy formulation. (This trip is funded). Each student produces an international and South African literature review for their proposed South African policy assessment exercise. At the end of the semester, each student submits a policy assessment paper and makes a presentation to the class. Feedback is given on the proposal, and structured feedback is provided during the writing of the policy assessment paper.

Prerequisite: GLBL 5020. Students are expected to be familiar with basic econometric/statistical methods through multivariate linear regression and to have experience with Stata. An undergraduate course in development economics is strongly recommended. The trip to South Africa is part of the course and compulsory.

202701:23651.text: The goal of this course is to provide a comprehensive exploration of the crucial roles that genomics and molecular pathology play in the field of precision medicine. This course covers a wide range of topics that are crucial for understanding the application of precision medicine for inherited, neoplastic, and infectious disease. Students will be introduced to fundamental concepts of human genomics and laboratory techniques used in molecular pathology, enabling them to analyze genetic and molecular information in clinical and research settings to advance precision medicine and personalized patient care. This course will be required in the spring semester of year 1 of the Master of Health Science in Clinical Investigation (MHS-CI) curriculum and will meet once a week for 3 hours in the afternoon for a total of 15 sessions. Each session will include both lecture and discussion components. For the first 75 minutes, a Yale faculty expert will use an interactive lecture format to introduce students to fundamental concepts and techniques in a specific area of molecular genomic pathology, highlighting applications in personalized medicine. Following a 10-minute stretch break, the next 75 minutes will be devoted to a journal-club style discussion of a pre-assigned research article that relates thematically to that week's faculty lecture. Each week, one student will serve as the designated journal club discussion leader and will prepare an oral presentation under the guidance of that week's faculty mentor; the remaining students will be expected to actively participate in discussion of the research article. Collectively, these activities will use a collaborative approach to develop skills in the critical analysis of molecular and genomic data relevant to precision treatment approaches. Permission of the instructor required.

202701:23672.text: This course explores the legal questions raised by historical and contemporary national security issues and policies. Learning the law is not as simple as learning set rules and applying them: there is rarely a “right” or “wrong” answer to a complex legal question. National security law, in particular, is an expanding field of study, with new laws and policies testing the limits of previously understood constitutional and legal boundaries. We therefore focus on how to approach national security questions by understanding the fundamental legal tenets of national security policies, the analyses used by courts and legislatures to confront various intelligence and terrorism issues, and theories of how to balance the interests of national security with civil liberties. Although the course is taught much like a traditional law class with an emphasis on the U.S. Constitution, statutes, regulations, executive orders, and court cases, no previous legal knowledge is expected or required.

202701:23707.text: This module is designed provide instruction in the skills of teaching, observation, feedback and writing an Educational Philosophy. Through active learner-centered classes, students will engage in practicing their teaching, presentation and observation skills with their peers while also providing and receiving effective feedback. As part of the exercise of writing an Educational Philosophy, students will take a Teaching Perspectives Inventory which will provide them with a personal profile of their teaching beliefs, intentions and actions. This module also exposes learners to medical education literature on teaching theory and practice for discussion and implementation. There are experiential components outside the classroom in which the student teaches a class in their area of clinical expertise, a trained faculty observer attends the class completing a validated Observation Form. The student and faculty observer meet afterward to review the form, debrief the teaching and the student receives actionable feedback to their teaching. In addition, students attend Graduate Medical Education (GME) Committee meetings led by the Senior Associate Dean for GME. In these meetings GME Program and Associate Program Directors review the performance of resident and fellow education programs and discuss proposals for innovations and new programs to enhance the trainee educational experience. After attending two GMEC meetings and a class by the Associate Dean for GME, the students write a reflection paper on a topic of their choice on GME education. This module provides active classroom learning combined with practical experiences in education for every level of learners who students will encounter in their career. This module has been designed to provide a safe environment where learners are free to seek direction, ask questions and explore possibilities with the support and encouragement of their faculty educators. Permission of the instructor required.

202701:23708.text: The role of US law enforcement in international affairs has matured immensely since WWII, with several inflection points that have informed the persistent evolution of its responsibilities and desired outcomes. Collaboration between US law enforcement agencies and strategic foreign partners has been, and remains, nuanced and complex, heavily impacted by shifting geopolitical environments, competing priorities within the global interagency community, and often requiring a whole-of-government approach. Impactful US law enforcement international operations require outside-the-box thinking, fluency in legal authorities, and sensitivities to the asymmetrical and unpredictable variables unique to any geographical region in which one operates. The goal of this course is to prepare students to think critically about the responsible leveraging of US law enforcement, in partnership with the broader US intelligence community and foreign partners, to hold responsible those who have committed criminal acts in violation of US federal law. This course explores real-world investigative and operational scenarios ranging from counternarcotics, counterterrorism, counterintelligence, crisis negotiation, and hostage rescue matters, analyzing each in search of more creative and efficient solutions, as criminal and terrorist enterprises continue to be a pacing global threat.

202701:23735.text: An independent study course for MHS students to explore a range of topics and issues related to bio-medical ethics and the ethical conduct of research. Completion of a self-directed online Responsible and Ethical Conduct of Research (RCR) course provides students with foundational knowledge of the norms, principles, regulations, and rules governing the practice of research. Students will complete the core modules for either the Biomedical Basic OR the Social-Behavioral-Educational Researchers Basic course (depending on the MHS track) and will also select a minimum of 4 supplemental modules selected by the track leader. A certificate of completion must be provided as evidence this requirement has been met. These self-directed modules are supplemented by exploration of ethics topics through existing Yale structures. Students will participate in four 1.5 hour bioethics seminars* curated from the existing bioethics elective for MD students. Students will also attend an ethics-focused lecture as part of the MHS program's BLISS series. In addition to these requirements, students will attend an additional 4 hours of ethics-related programming selected from existing ethics series at Yale, including the YSM Program for Biomedical Ethics Seminar Series or the Yale Law School Solomon Center for Health Law and Policy lectures. Students will maintain records of their attendance. Students will have the flexibility to select sessions that align most closely with their areas of interest and their research. Attendance at either a YNHH ethics or HIC meeting is another option toward meeting the 4-hour ethics programming requirement. Drawing on this coursework, students will write a brief reflection paper on an ethical principle(s) of their choice that relates to their scholarly work. Permission of the instructor required.

202701:23780.text: This course is designed for students wanting to deeply reflect on what it means to be a leader, and to help them prepare for leading others in their future. Amongst the many pressures of the role, leaders affect the lives of those they lead, influence the health of the organization they oversee, and hold an important role in advancing social progress. Many learn these realities through trial and error but are rarely given the time to consider what leadership truly entails and how we, as individual leaders, will handle the challenges that lie ahead. From heading up a small team to running a major organization, leadership is often an isolating and uncertain position, but is also full of opportunity to positively impact others, and to advance society broadly. Leadership is challenging, exciting, and sometimes terrifying; but most importantly, it is a choice to which one must recommit every day. This course is designed to offer a foundation in the practice of leadership for students who want to take on these challenges in their future. The course is divided into three main sections: historic perspectives on leadership, leadership in context, and personal reflections on leadership. Students finish the semester with a foundational understanding of leadership models throughout history, a range of case studies to refer to in the future, and most importantly, a personal framework that can be applied and expanded throughout their journey and growth as a leader. Students do not leave with all the answers they need to conquer the countless challenges that leaders face, but they instead leave with an understanding of how leaders work, every day, to improve themselves and better the lives of those they lead.

202701:23827.text: This course focuses on equipping students with useful tactics, tools, and strategies to more successfully engage the growing global space between governments, global institutions, NGOs, private companies and rebel groups. This course is designed to assist the process of delivering a more effective practitioner of international relations, empowered with the latest ideas. An emphasis is placed on bringing leading practitioners, in contrast to the traditional approach of current and former government officials, to class as well as engaging with actors currently on-the-ground in conflict and post-conflict zones.

During this elective, the master’s student will receive six hours of instruction in a small group setting with simulation faculty. Learning sessions will be divided in 2-3 hours sessions (depending on learner enrollment and schedules) and will include interactive small group learning on the foundations of medical simulation principles including:

-Pedagogy of simulation

-Simulation design

-Simulation operations

-Simulation debriefing

-Overview of subdisicplines in medical simulation (Simulated participants, Procedural simulation, Tele-simulation, Serious gaming, AR/VR/XR simulation)

Practicum experience:

The Yale Center for Healthcare Simulation (YCHS) is the simulation center for Yale School of medicine as well as Yale New Haven Health. YCHS hosts thousands of hours of medical simulation sessions for all members of the health care team including medical and PA students, residents, nurses, EMS, and more. The mission statement for YCHS is to provide excellent patient care through innovative medical education, assessment, research, system integration and outreach. Elective students will have the opportunity to participate in a wide variety of simulation activities including multiple modalities (such as high fidelity mannequin simulation, simulated particpants, telesimulation, virtual reality, procedural simulation, interprofessional simulation and in-situ simulation) with a wide variety of learners.

During this elective, learners will facilitate 3-12 hours of simulation sessions at YCHS. For each simulation session, learners will facilitate a simulation case under the guidance of a simulation faculty. Learners will perform all functions of simulation facilitation from pre-briefing, case facilitation, and debriefing. Learners will work with simulation faculty to schedule the simulation sessions. Simulation sessions occur throughout the week at YCHS Monday-Friday.

Meetings with the Faculty Elective Directors:

For each simulation session, learners in this elective will have 30 minutes of debriefing after direct observation with simulation faculty to provide feedback on simulation facilitation and debriefing. In addition, learners will have a 1 hour mid-point feedback session with simulation faculty to discuss specific feedback on points of improve and to set goals for future simulation sessions. This midpoint feedback session should occur after 1 observed simulation facilitation but before the final observed simulation session

Instructor approval required prior to enrolling in the course

202701:24297.text: This course continues work begun in Liturgical Keyboard Skills I (MUS 556) and delves more deeply into the hymnic and liturgical repertoire of American and European classical traditions. Focused on the accompaniment and leadership of congregational singing, the course systematically surveys the service music and hymnic repertoire of Catholic and mainline Protestant traditions in the U.S. Students continue building skills in strong leadership of congregational song and improvisational skills needed to support the accompaniment of the liturgy. Students will jointly lead an extended choral liturgy as a final project to the course. Prerequisite: MUS 556.

202701:24514.text: This graduate seminar examines the role of film as artwork that can be a tool of strategic communication and policy influence for domestic and global audiences. The course treats cinema—feature films, documentaries, and digital media—as both a reflection of political realities and an active agent in shaping public opinion, social relations, and policy agendas. It examines questions of how stories that illuminate pressing global policy issues can be effectively expressed through visual media. It studies select films and communication campaigns, both contemporary and historical, that have brought fresh awareness and, in some cases, concrete change, to pressing policy concerns. In this course, we examines documentary films as the main form of film, but we also discuss how fiction and crowd-sourced media phenomena can function to move audiences to new understandings and possibly avenues for change. Themes include realism, propaganda and persuasion, and investigative work. Students develop tools to critically evaluate visual media from the perspective of ethics, aesthetics and effectiveness. Assignments emphasize screening films, discussing subjective and objective truth in visual media, decoding cinema language and the underlying ethics. Coursework develops towards a final project that involves an in-depth exploration of one or more aspects of course themes. The course includes occasional special guest instructors and speakers who work in filmmaking, advocacy and communications.

202701:24515.text: This course examines the evolution of defense innovation in the United States and its allies and partners over the last fifteen years, and particularly efforts to leverage commercially derived technology and rapid technology development cycles in areas such as artificial intelligence, autonomy, space, biotechnology, energy, cyber/telecom, and advanced manufacturing for national security. We examine the origins and imperative for transformation in this arena, critical areas of tech and their impact, related policy and acquisition/procurement tools and structural reforms, the intersection between the Department of Defense (or “War”) and Congress, the evolution of the defense tech ecosystem’s founders and funders, operational integration and the perspective from the warfighter, lessons from the war in Ukraine and other recent conflicts, adversary approaches and threats, and the critical role of allies and partners. The course also provides students with the opportunity to explore remaining barriers, current efforts at reform, and potential solutions. Perspectives from current practitioners across the military, policy and legislative, and defense-tech sectors are incorporated, including through selected guest speakers.

202701:24555.text: This course equips students with an applied understanding of how artificial intelligence can cause or amplify harm, and how the actors who develop, deploy, and govern these systems can be held accountable. Across seven classes, the course takes an interdisciplinary approach, using disinformation and online manipulation as an entry point into broader questions of AI safety, power, and governance. We begin with the relationships among influencers, audiences, and algorithms that drive disinformation, then examine how propagandists use generative AI and synthetic media to shape public discourse and political outcomes. We turn to responses: the institutions and trade-offs of content moderation; product policies for text, image, and other generative AI systems; and competing approaches to technology regulation and self-regulation. The final two classes examine the alignment problem, including immediate and catastrophic risks, and the implications of AI agents and artificial general intelligence (AGI) for governing collective intelligence. Throughout, students ask who defines acceptable AI behavior, whose interests and rights are protected, and how responsibility should be allocated among companies, governments, and users. Through case studies, hands-on experimentation with generative AI, policy drafting, and a constitutional AI exercise, students develop tools to assess harms, evaluate safeguards, and design approaches to AI accountability that reflect societal values.

202701:24596.text: Earth system tipping elements, ecosystems that may have thresholds where small changes can provoke irreversible shifts to new, potentially very different, states, are increasingly recognized economic, security, and development risks. They are also hard to govern. They are foreseeable but not predictable. They are driven by both global warming and local pressures such as land use and pollution. Their impacts may appear only after a threshold is crossed, then cascade globally over decades. This half-term seminar focuses on one tipping element, the Amazon rain forest, as a case for exploring what such nonlinear risks demand of institutional design and policy strategy. It draws on comparative “risk repertoires” from terrorism, pandemics, and nuclear preparedness, on decision-making under deep uncertainty, and on current proposals for tipping-element governance to identify possible approaches to institutional design. It includes a spring-break field visit to Brazil that brings students into conversation with policymakers, scientists, and civil society working on tipping element governance. The seminar is demanding: its reading load exceeds a typical M.P.P. course. Assignments are designed to encourage substantive contributions to live policy discussions and require independent research beyond curated course materials.

We are at a historic moment in the development of AI, which brings us far-reaching application opportunities for policy work. This class invites students with serious professional pursuits to re-examine and prototype what is possible in their fields with deep AI integration. The first session reviews the foundations and practical tools introduced in the fall seminar, Applied AI for Global Affairs I (GLBL 5053), and introduces the goals for this second semester. We then conduct case studies on selected fall projects. Each week or two, the class receives a project folder with concrete data or source documents, working files, and a project report. Where available, the student author explains the path walked: data collection, early attempts, iterations, and important decisions. For primarily quantitative or technical work, students practice reproducing the project, an independent review, and a small investigation of a new aspect over the following week; for primarily qualitative work, a close read, critical review with annotations and recommendations for revisions or extensions would be warranted. Students are advised on best practices for agentic AI (including but not limited to coding), covering setup, context, tooling, iteration, and orchestration. For agent work, outcomes may vary, but within the cohort we critically compare our findings and reflect on our learnings as a group. Beginning midway through the semester, students develop their own independent projects, drawing on the methods practiced in the case studies. We welcome guest practitioners to examine our work at the intersection of AI and global affairs.

There are no formal prerequisites for this course, but students who have taken GLBL 5053 (Applied AI for Global Affairs I) are given priority consideration; prior AI experience is a plus.

Beginning with the earliest published sonatas and proceeding through detailed score study of examples from both small- and large-scale genres (sonata, suite, concerto, symphony, string quartet, concert overture, keyboard miniature, and symphonic poem), the course addresses a wide range of repertoire via historically grounded case studies and occasional forays into contemporary narrative theory. Composers addressed include Marini, Froberger, Biber, Kuhnau, Corelli, Vivaldi, Bach, Haydn, Beethoven, Mendelssohn, Schumann, Berlioz, Liszt, Hensel, Brahms, Rimsky-Korsakov, Strauss, Dukas, Dvorák, Debussy, Schoenberg, Still, Messiaen, Gubaidulina, Takemitsu, and Léon. Course requirements include weekly listening and short readings, occasional oral presentations (4-6 minutes) and brief response papers, a final project (a 5-8-page paper, a curated performance, or a model composition), and a final oral examination on topics chosen by the student.

202701:25132.text: 4 credits. NP. Group B. Behind today’s performance industry lies centuries of intersections between musicians and a music-loving public. 202701:25133.text: 4 credits. NP. Group A or B. This course looks at the arc of American experimentalism over the course of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries and is offered over two terms (though each of the two courses may be taken without the other as a prerequisite). 202701:25407.text: 4 credits. NP. Group A. Swing is not just a fundamental element of jazz, but one its most central contributions to Western music more broadly. Although sometimes characterized as a simple, uneven division of the quarter note, swing in fact describes a more pervasive and varied rhythmic quality of jazz performance practice, expressed through driving drum grooves, walking bass lines, syncopated comping rhythms, and flowing melodic lines. Swing is easy to feel but difficult to master: for many musicians, it represents the most challenging part of learning to authentically perform in jazz styles. This course develops students’ sense of rhythmic feel and groove in jazz and related popular styles and provides them with tools to understand what makes music swing. In addition to comparing swing with rubato and related concepts in the Western concert tradition, the course will build musicianship and interpretive skills that can deepen students’ musical practice. Students will develop knowledge of characteristic rhythmic vocabulary used to shape melodies, take apart drum grooves, examine microtiming in instrumental and vocal melodic lines, and analyze the rhythmic relationships between members of an ensemble to better understand what propels swing grooves in jazz and beyond.
